ind.prompt: Which benchmark is this fraction closest to?

sg.title: Why estimate?
sg.text:
Estimating gives you a **close** answer fast. It helps you check if your real answer makes sense.
Today we use three **benchmarks**: 0, ½, and 1.

sg.title: Notes: the three benchmarks
sg.text:
If the numerator is very small compared to the denominator, the fraction is close to [[0|zero]].
If the numerator is about half of the denominator, the fraction is close to [[1/2|½|half|one half]].
If the numerator is almost the same as the denominator, the fraction is close to [[1|one]].

sg.title: Teacher example
sg.text:
3/7 → ?
Step 1: Find half of the denominator. Half of 7 is **3½**.
Step 2: Compare the numerator. 3 is very close to 3½.
Step 3: So 3/7 is about **½**.

sg.title: Try it with me
sg.reveal: 8/9 ≈ 1 and 1/6 ≈ 0, so the sum is about **1**.

sg.title: In your own words
sg.text: How do you know if a fraction is close to ½?

days.title: Day 2: Rounding mixed numbers
days.target: I can estimate sums and differences of mixed numbers by rounding to the nearest whole number.

ind.prompt: Round to the nearest whole number.
Round to the nearest whole number.
Round to the nearest whole number.
A board is 8 5/6 feet long. Leo cuts off 2 1/10 feet. About how much is left?

sg.title: From fractions to mixed numbers
sg.text:
Yesterday we rounded fractions to 0, ½, or 1. Today we round **mixed numbers** to the nearest whole number.
The fraction part tells you which way to round.

sg.title: Notes: the rounding rule
sg.text:
If the fraction part is less than ½, the whole number stays the [[same]].
If the fraction part is ½ or more, round [[up]] to the next whole number.

sg.title: Teacher example
sg.text:
6 4/5 + 3 2/9 ≈ ?
Step 1: 4/5 is more than ½, so 6 4/5 rounds to **7**.
Step 2: 2/9 is less than ½, so 3 2/9 rounds to **3**.
Step 3: 7 + 3 = **10**.

days.title: Day 3: Estimating products
days.target: I can estimate products of fractions and mixed numbers and check if an answer is reasonable.

ind.prompt: A recipe uses 2 7/8 cups of flour. Sam makes 4 batches. About how much flour does he need?

sg.title: Estimating when we multiply
sg.text:
We can use the same rounding tricks to estimate **products** and **quotients**.
A good estimate helps you catch a wrong answer before you turn it in.

sg.title: Notes: multiplying by a fraction
sg.text:
When you multiply a number by a fraction less than 1, the answer gets [[smaller|less]].
To estimate with mixed numbers, round each one to the nearest [[whole|whole number]] number first.

sg.title: Teacher example
sg.text:
4 6/7 × 5 1/5 ≈ ?
Step 1: 4 6/7 rounds to **5**.
Step 2: 5 1/5 rounds to **5**.
Step 3: 5 × 5 = **25**. The real answer should be close to 25.

sg.title: Try it with me
sg.text:
2 9/10 × 7 ≈ ?
Tap the whole number 2 9/10 is closest to.
{{2 9/10}}
Estimate: [[21|twenty-one]]
